original_value: AbstractObjectiveReliable longitudinal risk prediction for hospitalized patients is needed to provide quality care. Our goal is to develop a generalizable model capable of leveraging clinical notes to predict healthcare-associated diseases 24–96 hours in advance.MethodsWe developed a reCurrent Additive Network for Temporal RIsk Prediction (CANTRIP) to predict the risk of hospital acquired (occurring ≥ 48 hours after admission) acute kidney injury, pressure injury, or anemia ≥ 24 hours before it is implicated by the patient’s chart, labs, or notes. We rely on the MIMIC III critical care database and extract distinct positive and negative cohorts for each disease. We retrospectively determine the date-of-event using structured and unstructured criteria and use it as a form of indirect supervision to train and evaluate CANTRIP to predict disease risk using clinical notes.ResultsOur experiments indicate that CANTRIP, operating on text alone, obtains 74%–87% area under the curve and 77%–85% Specificity. Baseline shallow models showed lower performance on all metrics, while bidirectional long short-term memory obtained the highest Sensitivity at the cost of significantly lower Specificity and Precision.DiscussionProper model architecture allows clinical text to be successfully harnessed to predict nosocomial disease, outperforming shallow models and obtaining similar performance to disease-specific models reported in the literature.ConclusionClinical text on its own can provide a competitive alternative to traditional structured features (eg, lab values, vital signs). CANTRIP is able to generalize across nosocomial diseases without disease-specific feature extraction and is available at https://github.com/h4ste/cantrip.

result.paraphrase: AbstractObjectiveReliable longitudinal risk prediction for hospitalized patients is necessary to support high-quality care. We aim to build a generalizable model that uses clinical notes to forecast healthcare-associated diseases 24–96 hours ahead.MethodsWe created a reCurrent Additive Network for Temporal RIsk Prediction (CANTRIP) to estimate the risk of hospital acquired (occurring ≥ 48 hours after admission) acute kidney injury, pressure injury, or anemia at least 24 hours before it is reflected in the patient’s chart, labs, or notes. Using the MIMIC III critical care database, we extract separate positive and negative cohorts for each disease. We retrospectively establish the event date with structured and unstructured criteria and use it as indirect supervision to train and evaluate CANTRIP on disease-risk prediction from clinical notes.ResultsOur experiments show that CANTRIP, using text alone, achieves 74%–87% area under the curve and 77%–85% specificity. Shallow baseline models perform worse across all metrics, while bidirectional long short-term memory attains the highest sensitivity but with substantially lower specificity and precision.DiscussionAn appropriate model architecture makes it possible to leverage clinical text for predicting nosocomial disease, outperforming shallow models and delivering performance comparable to disease-specific models reported in the literature.ConclusionClinical text by itself can serve as a competitive alternative to conventional structured features such as lab values and vital signs. CANTRIP generalizes across nosocomial diseases without disease-specific feature extraction and is available at https://github.com/h4ste/cantrip.
